Problems in Mexico

For years, many people from Mexico and Central America have crossed into the U.S., often seeking better lives. Some critics say their home countries encouraged this migration to reduce poverty and unrest at home. These critics argue that many migrants sent money back to their families, helping their home economies.

Now, the situation is changing. With tighter U.S. immigration policies and economic troubles, more migrants are returning to Mexico. This return is creating new problems there: more people competing for jobs, housing, and resources. In some places, locals are blaming American visitors for higher prices, but some analysts believe the real cause is the large number of returning migrants.

When you choose to ride a bicycle, you are making a powerful statement. You are choosing health over convenience, sustainability over consumption, and community connection over social isolation. A street full of cyclists is a street that is safer, quieter, and more vibrant. It is a place where neighbors are more likely to interact, where local businesses can thrive, and where the air is cleaner. Each person who chooses to pedal helps to reclaim our public spaces for people, creating a positive feedback loop that encourages even more people to join the movement.

The Sprakers Reformed Church: A Beacon on the Mohawk

The Sprakers Reformed Church, a simple white chapel with welcoming green doors, stands as a quiet testament to the history of the Mohawk Valley. Located in the hamlet of Sprakers, Montgomery County, its origins trace back to the late 18th century, with the first Protestant Dutch Reformed Church in the area established in 1790. The current structure was built in 1858 on land donated by the Spraker family, who were prominent early settlers of Palatine German descent.

The church's history is intertwined with the development of the region. In 1882, the construction of the West Shore Railroad necessitated moving the entire building to its present location. Its white siding was chosen to symbolize purity, and its green doors to represent everlasting life and a welcome to all. Today, this historic church has found a new purpose, serving as a beloved rest stop and a beacon of hospitality for cyclists traveling the Erie Canalway Trail, offering a place of peace and shelter.

The Erie Canalway Trail: A Path Through History

The 100-mile journey from Rome to Sprakers is a ride along one of America's most historic corridors. The Erie Canalway Trail, which follows the path of the original Erie Canal and the modern Mohawk River, is a mix of dedicated off-road stone dust paths and quiet on-road sections.

The segment from Rome to Utica is a gentle, 16-mile ride through wooded areas, passing by historic canal locks. From Utica, the trail continues eastward, closely following the Mohawk River as it winds through the valley towards Little Falls. The most dramatic scenery of this section is found near Sprakers, in an area known as "The Noses." Here, the river cuts a narrow gap between two steep escarpments, offering stunning views and frequent sightings of hawks and, occasionally, bald eagles. The trail is a living museum, a quiet path that allows the modern traveler to experience the same landscape that defined the westward expansion of the nation.

The Annual Pilgrimage: The "Cycle the Erie Canal" Tour

For over two decades, Parks & Trails New York has hosted the "Cycle the Erie Canal" tour, an eight-day, 400-mile supported bicycle tour from Buffalo to Albany. This annual event has become a pilgrimage for thousands of cyclists of all ages and abilities, transforming the trail into a vibrant, rolling community for a week each summer.

The tour is a "pay-per-play" event, offering a high level of support that makes the long-distance journey accessible to a wide audience. The organization transports baggage, provides rest stops with food and water, offers mechanical support, and arranges for overnight stays in "tent cities" in towns along the route, including Rome. The tour is a curated historical and cultural experience. It includes guided visits to key sites like the Fort Stanwix National Monument in Rome and the Women's Rights National Historic Park in Seneca Falls. For many, this annual tour is a highlight of their year, a chance to connect with fellow cyclists and immerse themselves in the rich history of New York State.
